p1.key: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid and is only slightly ionized, so it has far fewer ions in solution. HCl, NaOH and NH<sub>4</sub>Cl are fully dissociated and conduct well.

A conjugate pair differs by one H<sup>+</sup>: H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>/H<sub>2</sub>O (and CH<sub>3</sub>COOH/CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>). The other options pair species that do not differ by just H<sup>+</sup>.

A buffer needs a weak base and its conjugate acid. III is NH<sub>3</sub>/NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> directly. In II, HCl neutralizes half the NH<sub>3</sub>, leaving equal amounts of NH<sub>3</sub> and NH<sub>4</sub>Cl. I contains only a strong acid and a salt.

A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor. HNO<sub>2</sub> donates H<sup>+</sup> to NH<sub>3</sub>. NH<sub>3</sub> accepts the proton, so it is the base. Having lone pairs or lots of H atoms does not make something an acid.
Larger Ka means a stronger acid. 1 × 10−5 (HY) < 3 × 10−5 (HZ) < 1 × 10−4 (HX), so HY < HZ < HX.

Acid is added to the base, so pH falls. A weak base starts at a moderate pH (about 11), shows a gradual buffer region, and has its equivalence point below pH 7. B starts at pH 13 with a long flat section (strong base). A and C have pH rising.
When [HA] = [A−], [H+] = Ka = 1 × 10−5 mol dm−3, so pH = pKa = 5.
Propanoic acid is a weak acid (pH below 7), propan-1-ol is neutral, and propylamine is a weak base (pH above 7): III < I < II.
Diluting 10 cm3 to 100 cm3 lowers [H+] tenfold, from 10−2 to 10−3 mol dm−3, so the pH rises by 1 to 3.
The conjugate bases are the species formed when each acid loses H+: CH3COOH → CH3COO− and H3O+ → H2O.
The weakest acid has the smallest K<sub>a</sub>: phenol, 1.3 × 10<sup>−10</sup>, is just smaller than HCN at 4.9 × 10<sup>−10</sup>.

Sodium ethanoate is the salt of a weak acid and a strong base. The ethanoate ion accepts protons from water, giving OH<sup>−</sup>. KNO<sub>3</sub> is neutral, and MgCl<sub>2</sub> and (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> are slightly acidic.
pH = −log[H+]. A rise of 2 pH units means [H+] falls by 102: from 10−2 to 10−4 mol dm−3, a decrease by a factor of 100.
A weak acid is only partly ionized, so at the same concentration it has a lower [H<sup>+</sup>] and fewer ions. It therefore conducts less well. Neither property is the same.
Ka = [H+]2/[HA] = (2.0 × 10−3)2/0.10 = 4.0 × 10−5 (ionization is small, so [HA] ≈ 0.10).
A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base in similar amounts: ethanoic acid with sodium ethanoate. In B and C, equal amounts react completely and leave no buffer pair.
A conjugate pair differs by a single H<sup>+</sup>: CH<sub>3</sub>COOH / CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>. The other conjugate pair here is H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>/H<sub>2</sub>O.

Adding water dilutes an acid, lowering [H+], so the pH increases towards 7, not decreases. 1 mol dm−3 HCl has pH 0, universal indicator paper is a mixture of indicators, and dilute HCl conducts because it contains ions.
[OH−] = 1.00 × 10−3, so [H+] = Kw/[OH−] = 1.00 × 10−11 mol dm−3, giving pH = 11 (pOH 3).

KBr is the salt of a strong acid (HBr) and a strong base (KOH), so neither ion reacts with water and the solution is neutral. FeCl<sub>3</sub> and NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> are acidic, and Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is alkaline.
A Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) acceptor. Producing OH⁻ is the older Arrhenius idea, and donating protons describes an acid.
pH 3.0 gives [H+] = [A−] = 1 × 10−3 mol dm−3. Ka ≈ (1 × 10−3)2/0.1 = 1 × 10−5 (dissociation is small, so [HA] ≈ 0.1).
The reaction is A<sup>−</sup> acting as a base, so its constant is K<sub>b</sub> of the conjugate base. K<sub>a</sub> × K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>w</sub>, so K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>w</sub>/K<sub>a</sub>.
At equal concentration a weak acid has a lower [H+], so it reacts more slowly with carbonates or metals. It has a higher pH and needs the same amount of base for neutralization.

Ethanamide is neutral: the lone pair on N is delocalized onto C=O, so it is not basic, and it does not ionize as an acid. Ethanoic acid is acidic; sodium ethanoate (salt of a weak acid) and ethylamine give basic solutions.
Convert to pH: P = 8, S = −log(2 × 10<sup>−7</sup>) ≈ 6.7, R = 5, Q = 3. Increasing acidity means decreasing pH: P, S, R, Q.
A conjugate base is what remains after an acid loses H+: HSO4− → SO42− + H+. H2SO4 is the conjugate acid of HSO4−.

[H<sup>+</sup>] = √(K<sub>a</sub> × c) = √(1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> × 0.10) = 1.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol dm<sup>−3</sup>. [OH<sup>−</sup>] = K<sub>w</sub>/[H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>−14</sup>/10<sup>−4</sup> = 1.0 × 10<sup>−10</sup> mol dm<sup>−3</sup>.

I contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (salt). In II, 0.001 mol NaOH neutralizes half of the 0.002 mol CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, leaving equal amounts of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>, so it is also a buffer.
Strong acid HCl has the lowest pH (1), then weak acid CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (~3), then weak base NH<sub>3</sub> (~11), and strong base NaOH has the highest pH (13).
A weak acid is only slightly dissociated (II), so its conjugate base A− holds onto H+ more readily than water does (I). Because little HA dissociates, [H3O+] is much less than [HA], so III is wrong.
Conductivity depends on the concentration of ions. Ethanol does not ionize; ethanoic acid (weak) is only partly ionized; sodium ethanoate (ionic salt) is fully dissociated. Order: II < I < III.
Ka(HX) = Kw/Kb = 10−14/10−10 = 10−4. With [HX] = [X−], pH = pKa = 4.
Metal oxide + acid → salt + water (e.g. CuO + 2HCl → CuCl2 + H2O). Hydrogen gas forms when a metal reacts with an acid.

p1.key: A conjugate pair differs by one H<sup>+</sup>. HNO<sub>3</sub> gains a proton (acting as a base) to become H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, so these form a pair (as do H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>).
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (weak base + strong acid) is acidic; ammonium ethanoate (weak acid + weak base with similar K values) is about neutral; sodium ethanoate (weak acid + strong base) is basic.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: I: excess H<sup>+</sup> shifts equilibrium left, so colour A shows. II: [HIn] = [In<sup>−</sup>] only when pH = pK<sub>in</sub>, not necessarily at pH 7. III: a weak acid–weak base titration has no sharp pH change, so no indicator suits it.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: I gives a weak acid with its conjugate base (ethanoate). II neutralizes half the acid, leaving equal amounts of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>. III neutralizes all the acid, so no weak acid remains and it is not a buffer.
[OH−] = Kw/[H+] = 1.0 × 10−14 / 2.0 × 10−3 = 5.0 × 10−12 mol dm−3.
By definition pK<sub>a</sub> = −log<sub>10</sub>K<sub>a</sub>, just as pH = −log<sub>10</sub>[H<sup>+</sup>].

Adding acid lowers pH, so the curve falls. A weak base starts at a moderate pH (about 10–11, not 13) with a buffer region, and the equivalence point is below 7 because the conjugate acid is weakly acidic. B starts too high (strong base).

Carbonic acid is a weak acid and only slightly dissociated, so most remains as H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>. H<sup>+</sup> and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> are much lower, and the second dissociation to CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> is even smaller.

0.25 mol NaOH neutralizes half the 0.50 mol CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, leaving 0.25 mol acid and 0.25 mol ethanoate: a buffer. In D, 0.25 mol Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> supplies 0.50 mol OH<sup>−</sup>, neutralizing all the acid.

Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is a salt of a strong base and weak acid; CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> accepts protons from water forming OH<sup>−</sup>, so the solution is alkaline. NaCl is neutral; NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> salts are acidic.
In D, H<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> accepts a proton from CH<sub>3</sub>COOH to form H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, so it is a base. In A, B and C it donates a proton (acting as an acid).

Mg fizzes (H<sub>2</sub>) only with the acid (I); NaOH reacts exothermically with the acid but not the base (II). Both strong acid and strong base are fully ionized, so the lamp glows brightly in both (III fails).

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> donates a proton to HNO<sub>3</sub>, so it is the forward acid. In the reverse reaction H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> donates a proton to HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, so it is also an acid. HNO<sub>3</sub> acts as a base here.
NaOH is a strong base: [OH−] = 1.0 × 10−2 mol dm−3. [H+] = 10−14/10−2 = 10−12, so pH = 12.00 (pOH = 2.00).

NaCl (strong acid + strong base salt) is neutral, pH 7. HCl is a strong acid; hydrated Mg<sup>2+</sup> and especially Al<sup>3+</sup> ions are small and highly charged, so they make solutions slightly acidic.

An indicator changes colour around pH = pK<sub>a</sub> (where [HIn] = [In<sup>−</sup>]), so pK<sub>a</sub> lies within its range. Colour changes need not be at pH 7, and red is acidic only for some indicators.
HNO<sub>3</sub> is a strong acid (lowest pH), H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> a weak acid, NH<sub>3</sub> a weak base and Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> a strong base (highest pH).

K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is the salt of a strong base and a weak acid; CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> accepts protons from water, forming OH<sup>−</sup>. NaCl and Li<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> are neutral; NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> is acidic.
pH 10 means [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>−10</sup> mol dm<sup>−3</sup>; [OH<sup>−</sup>] = K<sub>w</sub>/[H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>−14</sup>/10<sup>−10</sup> = 10<sup>−4</sup> mol dm<sup>−3</sup>.
The strong acid starts at about pH 1. The equivalence point is below 7 (the conjugate acid of the weak base is acidic) and the final pH levels off near 9–10, not 13. A shows a strong base.
A larger K<sub>a</sub> means a stronger acid: chloroethanoic (1.38 × 10<sup>−3</sup>) > benzoic (6.31 × 10<sup>−5</sup>) > ethanoic (1.74 × 10<sup>−5</sup>).

Convert to the same scale: pK<sub>a</sub> 3 means K<sub>a</sub> = 10<sup>−3</sup>, larger than 10<sup>−4</sup>, 10<sup>−5</sup> and 10<sup>−6</sup>. The largest K<sub>a</sub> (smallest pK<sub>a</sub>) is the strongest acid.
The strong acid has higher [H<sup>+</sup>], so Mg fizzes faster (I) and the solution conducts better (III). Neutralizing a weak acid releases less heat because some energy is used to ionize it (II).

A conjugate pair differs by one H<sup>+</sup>: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>. H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> differ by two H<sup>+</sup>.
Since K<sub>w</sub> = [H<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>] = 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup> at 25 °C, taking −log gives pH + pOH = 14.0.

Ammonium chloride is the salt of a weak base and strong acid; NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> donates protons to water, giving an acidic solution. Ammonium ethanoate is about neutral, sodium ethanoate basic, and NaCl neutral.
pH is a log scale: each unit is a factor of 10. A rise from pH 4 to 7 means [H⁺] falls from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³, a decrease by a factor of 1000.

Al³⁺ is small and highly charged, so the hydrated ion [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]³⁺ releases H⁺, making aluminium sulfate solution acidic. NaNO<sub>3</sub> and KCl are neutral; sodium ethanoate is basic.
A conjugate acid–base pair differs by exactly one H⁺: CH<sub>3</sub>COOH / CH<sub>3</sub>COO⁻. The other pairs differ by two H⁺ (e.g. H<sub>2</sub>O and O²⁻, NH<sub>4</sub>⁺ and NH<sub>2</sub>⁻).

A weak acid–strong base titration (NaOH + CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) has an equivalence point above pH 7 (about 8–9) with the steep part in the basic range, so phenolphthalein (pK<sub>in</sub> ≈ 9.3) works but methyl orange (≈ 3.7) does not.
Dissociation is endothermic, so heating shifts equilibrium right and [H⁺] rises, lowering the pH. But [H⁺] still equals [OH⁻], so the water remains neutral.
The reaction is NH4⁺ acting as an acid (Ka of the conjugate acid). For a conjugate pair Ka × Kb = Kw, so Ka(NH4⁺) = Kw/Kb.
Smaller pK<sub>a</sub> means a stronger acid. Increasing strength = decreasing pK<sub>a</sub>: W (4.87), Y (4.86), Z (4.85), X (4.82).
Dilution 10 cm³ → 100 cm³ (factor 10): [H⁺] = 0.01 ÷ 10 = 0.001 mol dm⁻³ (HNO3 is strong). pH = −log(10⁻³) = 3.

At equivalence a strong base + weak acid gives a basic salt (CH<sub>3</sub>COO⁻ hydrolyses), so NaOH/CH<sub>3</sub>COOH gives pH > 7. Strong/strong gives pH 7; weak base/strong acid gives pH < 7; weak/weak is about 7.
[H⁺] = 10−pH: from 10⁻¹ to 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, a decrease by a factor of 100.
A conjugate base is formed by removing one H⁺ from the acid: HSO<sub>4</sub>⁻ → SO<sub>4</sub>²⁻ + H⁺. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is its conjugate acid.
Ka = [H⁺][CH3COO⁻]/[CH3COOH], so [H⁺] = Ka × [acid]/[salt] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 2.0/1.0 = 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.
Al³⁺ is small and highly charged, so [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]³⁺ is acidic and releases H⁺. Mg²⁺ is only slightly acidic, NaCl is neutral and KHCO<sub>3</sub> is basic.
An indicator changes colour when [HIn] = [In⁻], i.e. at pH = pKin (the colour change range is about pKa ± 1). So pH ≈ 4.0.

A Brønsted–Lowry base accepts H⁺. CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> accepts H⁺ from water to become CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>⁺, and NH<sub>2</sub>⁻ accepts H⁺ to become NH<sub>3</sub>. CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>⁺ is the conjugate acid.
In pure water H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻ always gives [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so water is neutral at any temperature. Here [H⁺] = √(4 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2 × 10⁻⁷, so pH ≈ 6.7, not 7.
10 % of 0.01 mol dm⁻³ dissociates: [H⁺] = 0.001 mol dm⁻³, so pH = −log(10⁻³) = 3.0. C assumes full dissociation.
Each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H⁺]. Rising 3 pH units means [H⁺] falls from 10⁻³ to 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³, a decrease by a factor of 1000.
A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base. Partly neutralizing HCOOH with NaOH produces HCOO⁻, giving an HCOOH/HCOO⁻ buffer. A, B and C contain a strong acid or no weak-acid/conjugate pair.

K<sub>w</sub> increases with temperature, so [H⁺] = √K<sub>w</sub> increases and the pH of pure water falls (≈ 6.8 at 37 °C) while it stays neutral. Ionization is therefore endothermic, [OH⁻] rises and conductivity increases.

A basic buffer is a weak base plus its conjugate acid: NH<sub>3</sub>/NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (from NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>). A, C and D each include a strong acid or strong base, or a strong acid with its salt.

CH<sub>3</sub>COONa is the salt of a strong base and a weak acid; CH<sub>3</sub>COO⁻ + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + OH⁻ makes the solution alkaline. NaCl is neutral, NH<sub>4</sub>Cl acidic and CH<sub>3</sub>COONH<sub>4</sub> roughly neutral.
Conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺: H<sub>2</sub>O/OH⁻ and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>/NH<sub>3</sub>. HCl and NaOH are an acid and a base that react together, not a conjugate pair.

A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base. I: half the CH3COOH is neutralized, leaving equal acid and CH3COO−. III: acid + its salt directly. II neutralizes all the acid, leaving only the salt. B.
A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton (H+) donor. A describes a base; B and C are properties, not the definition.
Fe3+ is small and highly charged, so the hydrated ion [Fe(H2O)6]3+ releases H+, making the solution acidic. KCl and NaNO3 are neutral; CH3COONa is basic. B.
H2SO4 donates H+ to CH3COOH, so H2SO4 is the acid and CH3COOH the base. On the right, CH3COOH2+ (conjugate acid) can give the H+ back to HSO4− (conjugate base). Order: base, acid, acid, base. D.

A buffer needs a weak acid/base and its conjugate. In C, 4.0 mmol HCl reacts with 6.0 mmol NH3, leaving 2.0 mmol NH3 and 4.0 mmol NH4+: a basic buffer. A and B contain only strong acid and strong base, and in D the HCl is in excess. C.
Sodium ethanoate is the salt of a weak acid and a strong base. CH3COO− + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH−, so pH > 7. NH4+ and hydrated Al3+ salts are acidic, and Na2SO4 is neutral. C.
Weak base + strong acid gives an equivalence point below 7 (the salt CH3CH2NH3+ is acidic). Choose an indicator whose pKa lies in the acidic steep part: bromophenol blue (4.1).

NaOH is a strong base (fully dissociated), but ammonia is weak and only slightly ionized. So 1.0 mol dm−3 NaOH has much higher [OH−], lower [H+], higher conductivity and higher pH. Note that D is also a true statement.
p1.flag: D also true: NaOH has higher [OH⁻]; ms gives C only

p1.key: CH3CH2NH2 + H2O ⇌ CH3CH2NH3+ + OH−. Kb = [CH3CH2NH3+][OH−]/[CH3CH2NH2]. Water is the solvent, so it is left out. B.
A larger Ka means a stronger acid. 1.74 × 10−5 (X) < 1.78 × 10−5 (Z) < 1.38 × 10−3 (Y), so the order is X < Z < Y.
Added OH− removes H+ (forming water). The equilibrium HIn ⇌ H+ + In− shifts to the right to replace H+, so more In− forms and more of colour B is seen.
Forward: H2PO4− donates H+ to CN−, so it is an acid. Reverse: HCN donates H+ to HPO42−, so it is also an acid. The acids are HCN and H2PO4−.
Ethanoic acid and carbonic acid only partially dissociate in water (weak). HCl is a strong acid that dissociates completely. A: I and II only.
In pure water [H+] = [OH−], so pH = pKw/2 = 14.54/2 = 7.27. The water is still neutral; pH 7.00 applies only at 25 °C.
For a conjugate pair, Ka × Kb = Kw, so Kb(F−) = 1.0 × 10−14/6.8 × 10−4.
Adding some NaOH converts part of the ethanoic acid into ethanoate ions, giving a mixture of weak acid and conjugate base: a buffer. HCl, NaCl and more ethanoic acid do not provide CH3COO−. A.
[Fe(H2O)6]3+ is acidic: the small, highly charged Fe3+ polarizes a coordinated water so that it releases H+. KNO3 is neutral; Na2CO3 and CH3COONa are basic. C.
A conjugate base has one H+ fewer than its acid: H2CO3 − H+ = HCO3−. CO32− is the conjugate base of HCO3−, not of H2CO3.

Lower pH means higher [H+]: pH 1 has [H+] = 0.1 mol dm−3 and pH 2 has 0.01, ten times less (not twice, so D is wrong). pH alone cannot tell us acid strength or total acid concentration, so A and B need not be true. C.

I: weak acid + its salt (equal amounts). II: half of the ethanoic acid (10 mmol) is neutralized by 5 mmol NaOH, leaving equal acid and ethanoate. III: 50 mmol NaOH is in large excess over 10 mmol acid, so it is just a strong base solution. A.
[Fe(H2O)6]3+ releases H+ (small, highly charged Fe3+), and NH4+ is a weak acid, so II and III are acidic. Na2CO3 is basic (CO32− accepts H+ from water). C.

Both acids are monoprotic with the same amount, so they need the same volume of NaOH. Ethanoic acid (weak) starts at a higher pH, and its equivalence point is above 7 (ethanoate is basic), so A, B and D are wrong.

An indicator changes colour over roughly pKa ± 1, so pKa lies within 3.0–4.6. Below pH 3 HIn dominates (yellow), so A and B are wrong. Weak acid + strong base has an equivalence point near pH 9, so bromophenol blue is unsuitable (D).

NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> contains the weak acid NH<sub>4</sub>⁺ (from a weak base), and Al<sup>3+</sup> forms the acidic hydrated ion [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>. CH<sub>3</sub>COOK gives a basic solution because ethanoate is the conjugate base of a weak acid.

A conjugate pair differs by one H⁺. H<sub>3</sub>O⁺ and H<sub>2</sub>O differ by one proton (as do CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH/CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COO⁻). The other options pair species from different pairs.

A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base in significant amounts. Propanoic acid with potassium propanoate works. With equal moles of KOH (C) the acid is fully neutralized, leaving no acid; nitric acid is strong.

Conjugate pairs differ by exactly one H⁺. H<sub>3</sub>O⁺ and OH⁻ differ by two protons. HNO<sub>3</sub>/NO<sub>3</sub>⁻, CH<sub>3</sub>COOH/CH<sub>3</sub>COO⁻ and HSO<sub>4</sub>⁻/SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> are all genuine pairs.
pH = −log[H⁺], so each unit rise in pH is a tenfold fall in [H⁺]. A rise of 3 units means [H⁺] decreases by 10³ = 1000.
Convert to one scale: HB has pKa = 3.0 and HD has pKa = 5.0. The lowest pKa (largest Ka) is the strongest acid: HA with pKa = 2.0.

0.010 mol ethanoic acid + 0.0050 mol NaOH leaves 0.0050 mol CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and 0.0050 mol CH<sub>3</sub>COO⁻: a weak acid with its conjugate base, a buffer. HCl is strong (A, C), and in D the acid is fully neutralized.

The equivalence volume depends only on the moles of acid: 25 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ monoprotic acid always needs 25 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Ethanoic acid has a higher initial pH and an equivalence pH above 7.
10 cm³ → 1000 cm³ is a 100-fold dilution, so [H⁺] falls from 0.10 to 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and the pH rises by 2 units to 3.0.
Dissociation of water is endothermic, so raising the temperature shifts it right: Kw and [H⁺] increase and the pH falls below 7. The water is still neutral because [H⁺] = [OH⁻].

0.10 mol CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + 0.050 mol NaOH leaves 0.050 mol of the weak acid and 0.050 mol CH<sub>3</sub>COO⁻: an acidic buffer. A is a basic buffer (NH<sub>4</sub>⁺/NH<sub>3</sub>), B has no conjugate base and in D the acid is fully neutralized.
NH<sub>4</sub>Cl is the salt of a strong acid and a weak base; NH<sub>4</sub>⁺ donates H⁺ to water, so the solution is acidic. Ethanoates and carbonates give basic solutions.

Conjugate pairs differ by exactly one H⁺: NH<sub>4</sub>⁺/NH<sub>3</sub> and HCOOH/HCOO⁻. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> differ by two protons (the conjugate base of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is HSO<sub>4</sub>⁻).

Acids react with reactive metals to give hydrogen, a flammable gas: Zn + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → ZnSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>. Carbonates give non-flammable CO<sub>2</sub>, and Cu is too unreactive to react with HCl.
A weak acid only partly dissociates, so [H⁺] is less than its concentration: [H⁺] < 1 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ (pH > 2). Then [OH⁻] > 1 × 10⁻¹² and pOH < 12, so B–D are wrong.

[Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is a small, highly charged hydrated ion that releases H⁺ from its water ligands, giving an acidic solution. KNO<sub>3</sub> is neutral; ethanoate and carbonate salts are basic.
D: 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol NaOH neutralizes half of the 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol CH3COOH, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa (half-equivalence). B is at equivalence; C has excess NaOH; A contains a strong acid.
The buffer region is the flat part of the curve before the equivalence point, where the weak acid and its conjugate base are both present; here the pH rises only slowly from about 4.5 to 5.5.
HNO<sub>3</sub> and KOH are strong: W pH = 1, X pH = 3, Z pOH = 3 so pH = 11, Y pOH = 1 so pH = 13. Order: W < X < Z < Y.
pKa + pKb = pKw = 14.00, so pKb = 14.00 − 2.79 = 11.21. The structure contains a –COOH group and a benzene ring (its N atoms are in amides, not amines).

II and III are each a weak acid with its conjugate base (ethanoic acid/ethanoate, methanoic acid/methanoate). H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is a strong acid, so H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/HSO<sub>4</sub>⁻ is not a buffer pair.

1.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH starts at pH 14. Ethanoate at equivalence (25 cm³) is basic, so the vertical jump ends above pH 7, and excess weak acid then gives a buffer around pH 5, not pH 0–1. Only C shows this.
1.0 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> NaOH has [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 1.0, so pOH = 0 and pH = 14. Universal indicator is purple at this pH. NaOH is a strong base, fully dissociated, so the solution conducts well.

In pure water [H<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>−</sup>] = √(5.48 × 10<sup>−14</sup>) = 2.34 × 10<sup>−7</sup> mol dm<sup>−3</sup>, so pH = 6.63. The water is still neutral, because [H<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>−</sup>].
The smaller the pKa, the larger the Ka and the stronger the acid. Chloroethanoic acid has the lowest pKa (2.87).

Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>COONa are salts of a strong base and a weak acid. Their anions hydrolyse to give OH<sup>−</sup>, so the pH is above 7. Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> comes from a strong acid and a strong base, so its solution is neutral.
In a weak acid–strong base titration the equivalence point is above pH 7 (about 8.7 here). Phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0) changes colour in this range. The other indicators change colour too early.

In each equilibrium the acid donates H<sup>+</sup> to become its conjugate base. CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>/HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> and H<sub>2</sub>O/OH<sup>−</sup> (I), HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>/H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O/OH<sup>−</sup> (II), and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>/NH<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O/H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> (III) are all paired and labelled correctly.
pH is a log scale: a difference of 2 pH units means a 10<sup>2</sup> = 100-fold difference in [H<sup>+</sup>]. The concentrations of the acids are not given, so you cannot say which acid is stronger.

K<sub>w</sub> increases with temperature, so the ionization of water is endothermic (II). At 25 °C [H<sup>+</sup>] is higher, so the pH is lower (III). Pure water always has [H<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>−</sup>], so I is false.
Kb describes a base reacting with water to produce OH−: B− + H2O ⇌ HB + OH−. F− + H2O ⇌ HF + OH− has exactly this form.

A buffer contains a weak acid with its conjugate base, or a weak base with its conjugate acid. I (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH/CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>) and II (NH<sub>3</sub>/NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) are buffers. In III, 0.005 mol NaOH neutralizes half of the 0.010 mol CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, leaving equal amounts of acid and ethanoate, which is also a buffer.
At pH 5.0, methyl orange is above its range (yellow), bromothymol blue is below its range (yellow), and phenolphthalein is colourless. So the mixture looks yellow.
Group 1 and heavier group 2 hydroxides, such as LiOH, KOH and Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub>, dissociate completely in water, so they are strong bases. Ammonia and ethylamine are weak bases.
For a conjugate acid–base pair, pKa + pKb = pKw = 14.00 at 298 K. So pKa(NH4+) = 14.00 − 4.75 = 9.25.
The larger the Ka, the stronger the acid. In increasing order: Y (9.33 × 10−6) < Z (1.47 × 10−5) < W (1.35 × 10−3) < X (4.47 × 10−2).

H<sub>2</sub>O donates H<sup>+</sup> (Brønsted–Lowry acid) and becomes its conjugate base, OH<sup>−</sup>. HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> accepts H<sup>+</sup> (base) and becomes its conjugate acid, H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>.
Butanoic acid and methanoic acid are weak carboxylic acids, and ethylamine is a weak base. Each other option contains a strong base or acid: Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub>, HNO<sub>3</sub> or NaOH.
For a conjugate pair, Ka × Kb = Kw. Taking −log of each side: pKa + pKb = pKw, so pKa = pKw − pKb.
The weakest acid has the smallest Ka: HClO (2.9 × 10−8). The weakest base has the largest pKb: C6H5NH2 (9.13).

A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base: CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> (from CH<sub>3</sub>COONa). HCl is a strong acid and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>'s first dissociation is strong, so A–C cannot act as buffers.

NH<sub>4</sub>Cl comes from a weak base and a strong acid, and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> donates H<sup>+</sup>. The hydrated Cr<sup>3+</sup> ion is small and highly charged, so it releases H<sup>+</sup> from its water ligands. CH<sub>3</sub>COONa gives a basic solution.

Adding 450 cm<sup>3</sup> of water to 50 cm<sup>3</sup> gives 500 cm<sup>3</sup>, a 10-fold dilution. [H<sup>+</sup>] falls from 10<sup>−4</sup> to 10<sup>−5</sup> mol dm<sup>−3</sup>, so the pH rises from 4 to 5.
The conjugate acid of HS− (adding H+) is H2S. pKa = 14.00 − 7.08 = 6.92, so Ka = 10−6.92. S2− is the conjugate base, and 6.92 is the pKa, not Ka.

0.00500 mol HCl reacts with 0.0100 mol NH<sub>3</sub>, giving 0.00500 mol NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> and leaving 0.00500 mol NH<sub>3</sub>. This is a weak base plus its conjugate acid: a buffer. In B the NH<sub>3</sub> is completely neutralized, and C and D contain a strong acid with no weak base.

A is the half-equivalence point, where [HA] = [A−], so pH = pKa. B is the equivalence point, which is above pH 7 for a weak acid–strong base titration. C is in the excess-base region. The buffer region is around A.

Methyl orange changes colour at pH 3.2–4.4, so it suits titrations with an acidic equivalence point: strong acid–weak base, such as HCl with NH<sub>3</sub>. C has an alkaline equivalence point, and D (weak–weak) has no sharp end point.

Both acids have the same concentration and volume, so the same amount of acid, and both react completely with Mg, giving the same total volume of H2. HCl reacts faster because it is strong and has a lower pH, which makes A and D wrong.

Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is the salt of a strong base and a weak acid; CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> accepts protons from water forming OH<sup>−</sup>, so pH > 7. CuSO<sub>4</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub> (hydrated metal ions) and NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> give acidic solutions.

CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup>. In dilute solution [H<sub>2</sub>O] is effectively constant and is left out, so K<sub>b</sub> = [CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>]/[CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>].
After mixing equal volumes, [acid] = 0.500 and [salt] = 0.250 mol dm−3. [H+] = Ka[HA]/[A−] = 1.30 × 10−5 × 0.500/0.250 = 2.60 × 10−5 mol dm−3.

An indicator changes colour around pH = pK<sub>a</sub>, so its pK<sub>a</sub> lies within the 6.6–8.2 range. In strong acid HIn dominates (yellow), so A and C are wrong; a strong acid–weak base titration has an acidic end point, so D is wrong.
Dissolved atmospheric CO2 forms the weak acid carbonic acid (CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3), lowering unpolluted rain to about pH 5.6–6. SO2 causes acid rain (pollution); O2 and N2 do not acidify water.
Nitric acid, HNO<sub>3</sub>, dissociates completely in water, so it is a strong acid. H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>COOH are weak acids and NH<sub>3</sub> is a weak base.
The ionization is endothermic, so at 50 °C equilibrium shifts right: Kw increases and [H+] > 10−7, giving pH < 7. Water is still neutral because [H+] = [OH−], so A and B are wrong.

K<sub>b</sub> refers to a base reacting with water to form its conjugate acid and OH<sup>−</sup>: NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup>. B is acid dissociation (K<sub>a</sub>); A and C are neutralizations.

The small, highly charged Al<sup>3+</sup> ion forms [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>, which releases H<sup>+</sup> and makes the solution acidic. Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, RbCl and KBr come from strong acids and strong bases, so they give solutions that are essentially neutral.

0.10 mol HCl converts 0.10 mol NH<sub>3</sub> to NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, leaving 0.10 mol NH<sub>3</sub>: a weak base with its conjugate acid, which is a buffer. In A, excess HCl leaves no NH<sub>3</sub>; B and C contain no conjugate pair.
Dilution factor = 1000/10.0 = 100, so [OH−] = 1.00 × 10−2/100 = 1.00 × 10−4 mol dm−3. pOH = 4, so pH = 14 − 4 = 10.
Compare pKa (smaller = stronger): phenol 10.0, glycine 9.87, butanoic acid 4.82, chloroethanoic acid −log(1.38 × 10−3) = 2.86. Increasing strength: phenol < glycine < butanoic < chloroethanoic.

pH = pK<sub>a</sub> when [HA] = [A<sup>−</sup>]. In A, 0.010 mol NaOH neutralizes half of the 0.020 mol CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, leaving 0.010 mol each of acid and ethanoate, so pH = 4.8. B and C leave no acid; D gives an unequal ratio.

Hydrated Fe<sup>3+</sup>, [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>, is small and highly charged and releases H<sup>+</sup>, making the solution acidic. CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> and Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> are basic; NaNO<sub>3</sub> is neutral.

A weak base (NH<sub>3</sub>) with a weak acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) gives no sharp pH jump at the equivalence point, so no indicator changes colour sharply. The other titrations involve at least one strong species and have a steep vertical section.

A weak acid is only partially dissociated, so there are few ions: poor conductivity. A 0.001 mol dm−3 strong acid would have pH 3, so a weak acid has a higher pH, still below 7, e.g. pH 5. pH 7 and 10 are not acidic.
Convert to pKa (lower = stronger): ClCH2COOH 3, CH3CH2COOH 5, C6H5NH3+ 4.6, C6H5OH 10. Increasing strength: phenol < propanoic acid < C6H5NH3+ < chloroethanoic acid.

An acid buffer is a weak acid plus its conjugate base: ethanoic acid with sodium ethanoate. HCl is strong (A); equal amounts of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and NaOH react completely, leaving no acid (C); D contains two weak acids.

Hydrated metal ions with a high charge density polarize water and release H<sup>+</sup>. Cr<sup>3+</sup> has the highest charge (+3) on a small radius (63 pm), so CrCl<sub>3</sub> gives the most acidic solution. Na<sup>+</sup> has no effect.

The buffer region is the flat part of a weak acid–strong base curve before the equivalence point, where both HA and A− are present (C, around pH = pKa). The strong-acid curve (A) has no buffer region; B is the equivalence jump; D is excess alkali.

A conjugate pair differs by one H<sup>+</sup>. H<sub>2</sub>O (base) gains a proton to become H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> (its conjugate acid). The other pair is CH<sub>3</sub>COOH/CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>; A, B and D mix species from different pairs.

A weak acid is only partly dissociated (I), so at equal concentration it has fewer ions and lower conductivity (III). Both strong and weak acids still react with metal oxides (neutralization), so II is false.

Adding acid to a strong base: pH starts high (~13) and falls. With a weak acid the equivalence point is above 7 (the ethanoate-type salt is basic), and after it the pH levels off at a weakly acidic value (~4–5), not ~1. Curve B shows this; C ends at a strong-acid pH.
HNO3 accepts a proton from H2SO4 to become H2NO3+, so it is a base. In the reverse reaction HSO4− accepts a proton from H2NO3+, so it is also a base.
Acid + hydrogencarbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide: 2NaHCO3 + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2H2O + 2CO2. Hydrogen is only formed when acids react with reactive metals.
B: 5.0 mmol NH3 + 2.5 mmol HCl leaves 2.5 mmol NH3 and 2.5 mmol NH4+, a weak base with its conjugate acid = buffer. In A the acid is in excess; C and D are strong acid + strong base.
CO32− is the conjugate base of a weak acid and accepts protons from water (CO32− + H2O ⇌ HCO3− + OH−), so Na2CO3 is alkaline. NH4Cl is acidic; the other two are neutral.
An amphiprotic species can both donate and accept a proton. H2PO4− and HPO42− both still have an H+ to lose and can also gain one. PO43− has no H to donate.
[OH−] = 1.0 × 10−3 mol dm−3, so [H+] = Kw ÷ [OH−] = 1.0 × 10−11 mol dm−3 and pH = 11. pH 3 would be the value for an acid of this concentration.
n(CH3COOH) = 2.0 mmol. Adding half that amount of NaOH (1.0 mmol = 10.0 cm3) gives equal amounts of acid and ethanoate, so pH = pKa ≈ 4.8. 40.0 cm3 would be excess NaOH, not a buffer.

A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor. A weak acid is only partially dissociated, so it produces few ions and its solution has poor conductivity compared with a strong acid of the same concentration.
Convert to pKa: chloroethanoic = −log(1.3 × 10−3) = 2.9; ethanoic = 4.8; HF = 3.3; HCN = 9.3. Smaller pKa means stronger acid: HCN < ethanoic < HF < chloroethanoic.
pH 10 means [OH−] = 10−4 mol dm−3. Diluting 10.0 cm3 to 1000 cm3 (100-fold) gives [OH−] = 10−6, pOH 6, pH = 8. Dilution of an alkali lowers the pH towards 7.
HCl partly neutralizes excess NH3, producing NH4+: a weak base with its conjugate acid is a buffer. A and C contain a strong acid; B contains a strong base with a weak-acid salt but no weak acid.

A weak acid is being added to a strong base (pH starts at 12, ends near 5.5), so the equivalence point is in the alkaline range (~pH 8–9). Phenolphthalein (pKa 9.6) changes colour within the steep part; the other indicators change below pH 5.
Methanoic acid is weak: only partly ionized, so [H+] ≪ 0.10 mol dm−3 and pH > 1. The statement "pH = 1" would be true only for a strong monoprotic acid, so A is incorrect.

A pKb of 4.1 indicates a fairly strong base: the tertiary amino N (N(C2H5)2), whose lone pair is readily available. The amide N's lone pair is delocalized into C=O, so it is barely basic; Cl and ether are not bases.
HPO42− can donate or accept a proton, so it is amphiprotic; any amphiprotic species can react as an acid or a base, so it is also amphoteric.
[H+] = Kw ÷ [OH−] = 10−14 ÷ 10−11 = 10−3 mol dm−3, so pH = 3. pH 11 would be the pOH.

A weak acid–strong base titration gives an alkaline equivalence point because the conjugate base hydrolyses: methanoic acid + NaOH → HCOO−, pH ≈ 8.5. A gives pH 7; B and C (strong acid + weak base) give pH < 7.

A strong acid gives up protons readily, so it is a good proton donor. Its conjugate base has little tendency to take the proton back, so the conjugate base is weak. Strong acid with strong conjugate base (A) is contradictory, and bases accept protons rather than donate them (D).
Convert to pKa: HF = −log(5.6 × 10−4) ≈ 3.3 and CH3CH2COOH = −log(1.3 × 10−5) ≈ 4.9. A lower pKa means a stronger acid, so increasing acidity is HClO (7.4) < CH3CH2COOH (4.9) < HF (3.3) < HIO3 (0.8).
In the forward reaction H2PO4− donates a proton to OH−. In the reverse reaction H2O donates a proton to HPO42−. OH− and HPO42− are the bases.

NH4Cl (weak base cation) is acidic; NaCl is neutral; CH3COONa (anion of a weak acid) is basic; CO32− is a stronger base than CH3COO− because HCO3− is a much weaker acid than ethanoic acid. Increasing pH: NH4Cl < NaCl < CH3COONa < Na2CO3.
When pH > pKa the indicator is mostly deprotonated, so [In−] > [HIn]. At pH 7 (above 5.1) colour B (In−) shows. At pH 3 HIn dominates (colour A), and [HIn] = [In−] only at pH 5.1.
Basic means [H+] < 1.0 × 10−7 mol dm−3 (pH > 7). [H3O+] = 1.0 × 10−13 gives pH 13. A and C are pH 3 and 4, and B has [OH−] = 10−13, so its pH is 1.

Acids react with hydrogencarbonates (giving salt, CO2 and water) and with reactive metals like magnesium (giving salt and H2). Calcium sulfate is a neutral salt of a strong acid and does not react as a base.
The weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base. HCN has by far the smallest Ka (6.2 × 10−10), so CN− is the strongest conjugate base.
NaOH is a strong base, so [OH−] = 10−3 mol dm−3. [H+] = Kw/[OH−] = 10−14/10−3 = 10−11, so pH = 11. pH 3 is the value you would get by confusing it with an acid of the same concentration.

The buffer region is the flat part of the curve before equivalence, where large amounts of both the weak acid HA and its conjugate base A− are present: region B. C is the equivalence point, and D is excess strong base.
The ionization of water is endothermic, so raising T shifts the equilibrium right: Kw and [H3O+] increase, so pH decreases. Water is still neutral because [H3O+] = [OH−].
A conjugate acid and its base differ by a single proton (H+), e.g. NH4+/NH3. A hydrogen atom includes an electron, so D is wrong.
HPO42− can donate a proton (forming PO43−) or accept one (forming H2PO4−), so it is amphiprotic. Al2O3 is amphoteric but has no H to donate, and CO32− can only accept protons.
pKa: CHCl2COOH = −log(5.0 × 10−2) ≈ 1.3; butanoic 4.8; propanoic 4.9; H3BO3 ≈ 9.2. A lower pKa means a stronger acid and lower pH: CHCl2COOH < butanoic < propanoic < H3BO3.
A Brønsted–Lowry base needs a lone pair to accept a proton. CH<sub>4</sub> has no lone pairs; HPO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>, H<sub>2</sub>O and NH<sub>3</sub> can all accept H<sup>+</sup>.

NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is the conjugate acid of a weak base and donates H<sup>+</sup> to water, so NH<sub>4</sub>Cl solution is acidic. CH<sub>3</sub>COONa and Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> are basic; KBr is neutral.

Dilution shifts NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup> to the right (more particles in solution), so n(OH<sup>−</sup>) increases slightly; but the volume increases much more, so [OH<sup>−</sup>] decreases.
Kc < 1, so the reverse reaction is favoured: H3O+ donates protons more readily than H3AsO4, making H3O+ the stronger acid.
Equivalence is at 50 cm3; at half-equivalence (25 cm3) pH ≈ 9.2 = pKa of the conjugate acid. pKb = 14 − 9.2 = 4.8.

Conductivity falls as ions are removed (insoluble BaSO<sub>4</sub> and water form), reaching nearly zero at equivalence (20 cm<sup>3</sup>), then rises as excess H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> adds H<sup>+</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> ions.
Conductivity depends on the ions present: the smaller the pK<sub>b</sub>, the stronger the base and the more ions it forms. Ethanol (15.5) < phenylamine (9.13) < methylamine (3.34).

A weak base starts at moderately high pH (≈11), has a gently sloping buffer region, then a short steep drop with equivalence below pH 7. A is strong base/strong acid; C ends above 7; D has no sharp jump (weak acid).
A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base in similar amounts, made by partially neutralizing a weak acid with a strong base. Complete neutralization leaves no weak acid.

At 10 °C: [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1 × 10<sup>−7</sup>, [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 3 × 10<sup>−15</sup>/10<sup>−7</sup> = 3 × 10<sup>−8</sup>, so [H<sup>+</sup>] > [OH<sup>−</sup>]. At 98 °C: [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 5 × 10<sup>−13</sup>/10<sup>−7</sup> = 5 × 10<sup>−6</sup>, so [H<sup>+</sup>] < [OH<sup>−</sup>].
